Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for evidence-grounded knowledge-base writing from 100 OMIM phenotype entries (2-12 references each). Each entry is drafted from its header and exactly the papers its curators cited (19% readable in full, the rest abstract- or title-only), with the causal gene withheld. One model (Claude Opus 5.5) writes every draft under several generation strategies: direct long-context reading, an agentic curator with read/search tools, an evidence graph, a case table, recall-then-verify, a memory-only control, and three add-ons (second-hand evidence, a reconciled case database, a learned curation guide). All drafts go through the same claim-level audit and repair, and are scored with the same model family against fixed fact lists split once from OMIM allelic-variant descriptions deposited in ClinVar (6,652 facts over 476 paragraphs). Secondary measures are HPO synopsis terms, variants, causal gene and inheritance. Main findings: (i) hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (paired +43.7 points); (ii) on facts that a model judges the supplied text to state, direct reading, the agentic curator and the evidence graph convey 93.6-94.4%, and on facts it does not state they convey 5.5-6.9%; (iii) between strategies, only case table first is reliably behind direct reading (-1.9 points), and a matched ablation largely erases that gap (-0.2); (iv) measurement choices, such as an asymmetric completion rule, produce spurious differences larger than those between strategies. Other parts include an audit planted-error test, a creation-date contamination check and per-entry release of drafts and scores.
Strengths: Unusually careful experimental control: same papers, same model, same guards, same audit and same scoring across strategies, with completion treated as an outcome and an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 8). The paper is candid that an earlier asymmetric completion rule produced a spurious 2.1-point gap (App. I.4). That lesson is useful to anyone comparing pipelines that make different numbers of calls.

Fixing the fact lists once, without sight of any draft, removes a real and often-ignored source of denominator drift in FActScore-style evaluation. The paper also quantifies the effect: per-draft splitting scores 2-5 points higher (Table 6).

The hidden-full-text manipulation is a clean within-paper experiment: the same 2,120 facts, no arm repaired, and 45 of 46 entries moving the same way. Its effect size is large enough to survive plausible judge noise.

The statistics are reported transparently: paired bootstrap intervals over entries, better/worse/tied counts, sign tests and Holm correction. Replicate noise (three replicates on 30 entries) and judge variation are reported separately, and the paper shows explicitly that a 30-entry subset reverses the sign of the evidence-graph difference.
Missed and conveyed facts are attributed to whether the supplied text states them (Tables 16-17), which turns an aggregate coverage number into a diagnosis of where the shortfall comes from.

Contamination is handled sensibly: a memory-only control stratified by creation era, plus 20 entries created after the strategies were developed. Memory-only coverage drops to 5.7-7.0% on the newest entries, and the paper rightly does not overclaim that reading is memorisation-free.

The paper is honest about scope: the limitations list is extensive, claims are hedged to the regime tested, and the observational access-group analysis is labelled as such, with an explicit refusal to claim that strategies separate where more full text is available.
Costs per entry are reported, and the harness, drafts, verdicts and scores are released.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement. Fact splitting, present/partial/absent marking, the 'stated in supplied text' judgement, the audit verdicts and the draft-reference disagreement checks are all made by the same model family that wrote the drafts. For a benchmark contribution this is the central methodological gap. Even a small curator-annotated sample (e.g., 200-300 fact judgements, plus 100 'stated' judgements) would establish whether the instrument measures what it claims. Judge self-consistency (95.7% agreement across rejudgings) measures reliability, not validity.

There is a possible circularity in the 'stated facts' analysis (Sec. 4.3, Table 2). Whether a fact is 'stated' in the text and whether it is 'conveyed' by a draft are both model judgements, likely made with similar lexical cues. A draft that paraphrases the abstract closely is then near-guaranteed to be scored as conveying what the same model found in the abstract. The ~94% ceiling and the 5.5-6.9% floor may partly reflect correlated judge behaviour rather than reading quality. This analysis carries the headline 'access bounds agreement' claim beyond the hidden-full-text experiment, so it needs either human checks or a judge from a different model family.

Only one model, and one proprietary model family, is used for everything. The paper's main substantive conclusion, that strategies matter little relative to access, may be specific to a frontier long-context model on inputs that fit one prompt. A weaker or open model, or one with a shorter context, could show larger differences between strategies. Without at least one other writer model, the generality claimed in the measurement lessons is not established for ICLR's audience.

The regime is narrow: 2-12 references, mostly abstracts, all inputs fitting one prompt. In exactly this regime, extract-then-write and agentic designs are least expected to help. The setting where those designs are motivated (many papers, long full texts) appears only in a 10-entry exploratory tier from which no conclusions are drawn. 'Strategies are close' is therefore close to expected given the design.

The primary reference is narrow and indirect. OMIM allelic-variant paragraphs are variant-centred, and only ~24% of a draft's statements have a counterpart in them (App. H). Most of what a draft says is checked only by a same-model fidelity audit, never against curator content. The endpoint thus measures recall of variant-level facts, not the quality of an entry.

There is a tension between the conclusion and the evidence on case table first. The abstract, Sections 4.2-4.4 and the Conclusion present 'case table first falls behind', but the matched ablation (Sec. 4.7) moves it from -2.3 to -0.2 against direct reading, and the paper attributes the gap to extraction effort in its own implementation. The defensible conclusion is about this implementation at medium extraction effort, not about the case-table paradigm.

The strategies are the authors' own implementations, and published systems (e.g., GraphRAG, PaperQA2, STORM) were not run. That limits the paper's value as a comparison of 'system designs'. Effort was matched in the ablation only for the extract-then-write arms, so it is unclear whether other implementation choices favour direct reading.

The primary endpoint is not adjusted for multiplicity across the five comparisons against direct reading, and several conclusions rest on intervals that 'touch' zero (agentic curator, -1.3 to +0.0) or on secondary restrictions. Given that the replicate-noise half-width (1.0 point) is comparable to most of the reported differences, a single run per entry is thin support for any ranking among reading strategies. The paper mostly acknowledges this, but it would be cleaner to report three runs for the main comparison.

Fit and accessibility for ICLR: the contribution is a carefully executed domain evaluation with no new method. Its general ML lessons (symmetric completion handling, fixed fact lists, conditioning on what the source states, reporting run-to-run noise) are sound but modest and partly known. The writing is extremely dense with numbers and qualifiers. Sections 4.1-4.4 are hard to follow without repeatedly consulting the appendix, and the main narrative would benefit from fewer inline statistics and a clearer statement of the 2-3 takeaways for ML practitioners.

Reproducibility depends on a proprietary model accessed through a CLI with no temperature or seed control, and on caching. Exact regeneration is impossible (acknowledged). Curator text is not redistributed, so others must rebuild the reference under OMIM's terms.
Questions: Can you provide any human validation, even small, of (a) fact present/partial/absent judgements, (b) the 'stated in supplied text' judgements and (c) audit verdicts? Agreement between a curator or domain expert and the model on a few hundred items would substantially strengthen the benchmark claim.
Did you try a judge from a different model family for the scoring and 'stated' judgements, at least on the 30-entry replicate subset? How much do levels and differences move?

How correlated are the 'stated' and 'conveyed' judgements at the item level beyond what reading explains? For example, on stated facts, how often does a draft use near-verbatim wording from the source sentence, and does coverage drop for paraphrased conveyance?

Given that the matched ablation removes most of the case-table-first deficit, would you revise the abstract and conclusion to attribute the gap to the implementation's extraction effort rather than to the paradigm?
Would any of the strategy differences emerge with a weaker or shorter-context writer model? Is there a reason to expect the 'access dominates strategy' conclusion to transfer?

For the hidden-full-text experiment, the full-text arm is the main run's draft while the abstract arms are newly generated. Were the abstract-arm prompts otherwise identical, and were they generated with the same model version and settings?

Since the primary reference covers only ~24% of draft statements, what fraction of the remaining 76% would a curator consider correct and appropriate for an OMIM entry? Is there any proxy for this beyond the same-model fidelity audit?

How sensitive is the primary endpoint to the half credit for 'partly present'? Table 6 gives full-only numbers; do the orderings and intervals hold under full-only scoring for the stated-facts restriction?
Limitations: All judgements come from one model family with no human validation (acknowledged); possible self-preference and correlated judge errors.
There is a single writer model, and the results may not transfer to other models or context lengths.
The regime is restricted to small reference lists and inputs that fit one prompt; settings motivating extract-then-write and agentic designs are not tested.
The reference covers mainly variant-level facts; most draft content is evaluated only by a same-model fidelity audit.
Only open-access text without supplements is used; recall and reading cannot be separated for facts stated in abstracts.
The strategies are the authors' implementations, not published systems.
There is a single run per entry for the main comparison; replicate noise is comparable in size to most between-strategy differences.
Generated entries could be mistaken for curated clinical content; the authors appropriately state that drafts must be labelled as machine-generated and not as OMIM content.
Thought: Very rigorous within its own frame: fixed fact lists, symmetric completion, paired bootstrap, replicate noise, and a clean hidden-full-text experiment (+43.7, 45/0/1) that I believe. I checked the numbers for internal consistency: Table 1 vs Tables 6/7/18, Figure 2 pooled counts (495+331/2 over 2,120 = 31.2%), the Figure 3 shares against Table 16, and the 52.2% in Sec. 4.6, which refers to direct reading on the 2026 set (Table 28). All consistent. The problem is that the instrument is never validated: every judgement, including the 'stated' restriction behind the second pillar of the headline claim, is made by the writer's own model family. That restriction is plausibly circular. There is also one writer model, and the regime (small reference lists, mostly abstracts, fits in one prompt) is one where strategy differences are least expected, so 'strategies are close' is near-expected. The case-table-first headline is undercut by the authors' own matched ablation. The paper reads more as an excellent domain evaluation report than an ICLR contribution with general ML insight; the measurement lessons are sound but modest. Presentation is precise but very dense. Borderline, leaning reject; a human-validated subset and a second writer or judge family would move me to 6.
